summary: Solomon Islands no longer issues visitor permits on arrival: every visitor must apply online before travel and show the grant letter at the border. The standard route is the 3-month Tourist Visa (USD 50 plus USD 50 lodgement); the Immigration Division also offers a free 30-day, single-entry Tourist Permit (USD 50 lodgement fee) but does not say which nationalities may use it. EU, Chinese, Hong Kong and Emirati citizens get a fee-free mutual exemption.

payments.text: The UK FCDO says only major hotels and restaurants in Honiara accept international credit cards, ATMs are only in Honiara, Gizo, Munda and Auki, and banking is difficult in rural areas. Australia's Smartraveller says cash is the primary currency outside Honiara.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says robberies involving violence, handbag snatching and pickpocketing happen, particularly around the central market and local beaches, and that foreign nationals are often targeted in the settlements around Honiara, White River, Lungga Bridge, Burns Creek and the airport area. It says demonstrations during sittings of Parliament and elections can turn violent quickly and that police have limited resources, and advises staying alert at night and avoiding political gatherings.

tips.text: The Government of Canada says malaria is a risk in the Solomon Islands and recommends antimalarial medication for most travellers — see a health professional before you go, and protect yourself from mosquito bites.

The UK FCDO says ATMs are only in Honiara, Gizo, Munda and Auki, that only major hotels and restaurants in Honiara accept international credit cards, and that you should have several ways to access money.

The UK FCDO says land ownership is an important and sensitive issue: on some hiking trails and many beaches around Honiara you may need to pay a fee ('kastom') to the landowner, and some 'tabu' sites have restricted access. Ask for local advice before setting off.

The free Tourist Permit covers a single entry of up to 30 days and cannot be extended. For anything longer, apply for the 3-month multiple-entry Tourist Visa instead, which can be extended in Honiara for USD 100.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Solomon Islands?
faq.answer: Yes, in the sense that everyone must now be approved online before travel: Solomon Islands no longer issues permits on arrival. Apply for the 3-month Tourist Visa (USD 50 plus USD 50 lodgement) or the free 30-day Tourist Permit (USD 50 lodgement fee); the Immigration Division does not say which nationalities may use the permit. EU, Chinese, Hong Kong and Emirati citizens apply for a fee-free mutual exemption.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Solomon Islands as a tourist?
faq.answer: Up to 30 days, single entry, on the free Tourist Permit, which cannot be extended. The Tourist Visa allows 3 months per entry, multiple entries over a year, and can be extended in Honiara. EU and Emirati citizens on the mutual exemption may stay up to 90 days.

faq.question: What do I need to show at the border?
faq.answer: Your e-visa grant letter, a passport valid at least 6 months, a return or onward ticket, a hotel booking confirmation if you stay at a hotel, and sufficient funds to support yourself.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay?
faq.answer: Not on the 30-day Tourist Permit. The Tourist Visa can be extended: apply at the Immigration Division's visa counter in Honiara well before your current entry permit expires and pay the USD 100 extension fee at the Finance and Treasury cashier.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate?
faq.answer: Only if you are aged 9 months or over and arriving from a country with a risk of yellow fever transmission. The Government of Canada also recommends antimalarial medication for most travellers.
